input_text:
A 36-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy underwent a live-related renal transplant 6 months ago and has been maintained on tacrolimus 3.5 mg daily, mycophenolate sodium 720 mg daily, and prednisolone 7.5 mg daily. He presented with a 14-day history of low-grade fever, dry cough, and anorexia without dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, or weight loss. He was afebrile on admission, heart rate 88 beats/min, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Examination revealed bilateral inspiratory crackles; other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL; total lymphocyte count 9900/μL; absolute neutrophil count 7720/μL; platelets 285 000/μL; serum creatinine 1.05 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated PaO₂ 68 mm Hg and an A–a gradient of 22 mm Hg. HIV ELISA was negative. Chest radiograph revealed bilateral diffuse alveolar infiltrates. High-resolution CT of the chest showed bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities without pleural or mediastinal abnormalities.

Sputum induction was non-diagnostic. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii on Grocott’s methenamine silver stain and negative for acid-fast bacilli, CMV inclusion bodies, and fungal hyphae. He was treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and a prednisone taper, with clinical and radiographic resolution of infiltrates after 2 weeks.

Three weeks into therapy, he was asymptomatic except for an occasional dry cough. TMP-SMX was discontinued, and prednisolone was maintained at 10 mg daily. Laboratory studies then showed leukopenia (TLC 1400/μL; ANC 1050/μL). Chest radiograph revealed new left upper-zone infiltrates. Repeat HRCT showed resolution of ground-glass opacities and new patchy peribronchovascular consolidations in the right upper lobe, left upper lobe, and left lower-lobe apical segment. Repeat BAL was negative for AFB, fungus, and Pneumocystis jirovecii. 

Transbronchial lung biopsy from the left upper lobe showed alveoli filled with inflammatory debris consisting of granulation tissue, interstitial inflammation, and areas of intra-alveolar fibrin deposition.

Atypical bacterial pneumonia was considered but not supported
Organizing pneumonia was supported by histopathology and timing
Secondary (postinfectious) OP related to PCP was favored over cryptogenic OP

input_text:
A 55-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and opioid use disorder presented with worsening abdominal distention and a 60-lb unintentional weight loss over 1 year, along with increasing difficulty with bowel movements. He denied melena, nausea, vomiting, fevers, flank pain, dysphagia, or odynophagia, and had no history of abdominal surgery.

Three weeks before admission, abdominal CT with contrast showed a small-bowel obstruction with a transition point in the right-mid abdomen and focal small-bowel wall thickening, plus mesenteric adenopathy. His symptoms improved without intervention, and he was discharged.

He returned 3 weeks later with diffuse abdominal pain. Repeat CT showed multiple dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. Colonoscopy revealed two polyps; cold-forceps biopsies showed non-specific chronic inflammation without features of inflammatory bowel disease. Video capsule endoscopy demonstrated erythematous gastritis, multiple small-bowel ulcers, and an atrophic duodenum. Two weeks later, double-balloon enteroscopy identified multiple jejunal strictures and areas suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease, and outpatient IBD management was planned.

Two months later, he presented with severe abdominal pain, new nausea, and vomiting. Abdominal radiographs suggested pneumoperitoneum. Exploratory laparotomy revealed a perforated ulcer in the terminal ileum, which was repaired, and a proximal Brooke ileostomy was created. Biopsies around the perforation showed ulcerated mucosa with non-specific chronic inflammation. He was discharged after a 21-day hospital stay.

One month later, he was re-hospitalized for non-specific abdominal symptoms and increased ostomy output. Ileoscopy showed scalloped mucosa with blunted villi throughout the ileum, and biopsies were taken. Histologic examination revealed extensive lymphocytic infiltrates with epitheliotropism but no definitive atypical morphological features, raising suspicion for a lymphoid neoplasm. A hematopathology consultation was obtained.

No dysphagia, other masses, or lymphadenopathy were detected. A CBC showed mild leukocytosis (23,690/µL; reference 8,700–17,500/µL) with neutrophilia (92.4%; reference 42.4–76.4%) and lymphopenia (3.0%; reference 7.0–32.5%); eosinophils were decreased; hematocrit was 39.8% (reference 27.0–39.0%), MCV was mildly increased, and MCHC was mildly decreased. Flexible endoscopy of the esophagus and trachea under sedation revealed no abnormalities. Cervical ultrasonography showed a well‐demarcated, heterogeneously echogenic, encapsulated mass with no communication with the trachea or esophagus and no intrinsic vascular flow. Thoracic and cervical radiographs demonstrated a ventral soft‐tissue‐density mass in the mid‐to‐caudal cervical region causing a mild mass effect on the trachea; no pulmonary lesions or further abnormalities were noted.

On examination, blood pressure was 113/70 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, and temperature 37.5 °C. Abdominal, cardiorespiratory, neurological, and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 13 mm gestational sac with irregular margins and a yolk sac in the anterior isthmic portion of the uterus, raising suspicion for a cesarean-section scar ectopic pregnancy. She was taken to laparoscopy and hysteroscopy: the bladder was densely adherent to the anterior uterine wall, the ectopic was not visualized, and extensive intrauterine adhesions obscured the view; there was no intracavitary bleeding. Postoperatively, she became hypotensive (systolic 82–95 mmHg) without vaginal bleeding. This prompted an urgent MRI to map the location of the pregnancy.

A 66-year-old white man presented to the Emergency Department with abrupt onset of dyspnea, palpitations, and lightheadedness. In the ED, he was found to be in monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and was electrically cardioverted into normal sinus rhythm. His medical history included a cerebrovascular accident, Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations, hypertension, incidentally noted pulmonary nodules, and chronic kidney disease (baseline GFR 40–45 mL/min/1.73 m2). He was taking losartan and warfarin and had no family history of sudden cardiac death.

Initial laboratory studies were within normal limits, and coronary angiography ruled out ischemia. His electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes, but an epsilon wave in V1, a QRS duration of 140 ms, and T-wave inversions in leads V1–V5. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved left ventricular function and no valvular disease, but a markedly dilated right ventricle with severely reduced systolic function. Based on an epsilon wave in V1–V3, T-wave inversions in V1–V3 with QRS >110 ms, an RV outflow tract dimension >32 mm, and severe RV dilation and hypokinesia, arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia was highly suspected. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was indicated but not performed because of chronic kidney disease and patient preference. A septal endomyocardial biopsy was considered but deferred due to its low yield. Given the patient’s pulmonary nodules, cardiac sarcoidosis remained in the differential diagnosis.

input_text:
An 89-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) and hypertension presented with acute speech disturbance and right-sided weakness. On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative. 

Noncontrast head CT showed early ischemic changes in the left insula and frontal lobe. CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory. 

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein (10.74 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL) with normal renal, liver function, and electrolytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis (10 cells/µL) and elevated protein (55 mg/dL) with normal glucose. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.

input_text: A 78-year-old man with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, a history of moderately differentiated prostatic adenocarcinoma without evidence of metastasis, and nodular basal cell carcinoma presented with a lesion on the glans penis. On examination, there was a 2 × 2 cm irregular, friable mass on the glans. A deep shave biopsy showed nearly complete epidermal ulceration with replacement by an in-situ and diffusely infiltrative atypical clear cell tumor. Within the epidermis, the cells displayed diffuse pagetoid spread. The tumor consisted of large irregular nests and lobules of clear cells with abundant multivacuolated cytoplasm, nuclear indentations, and vesicular to hyperchromatic nuclei. Lymphovascular invasion was present. The initial differential diagnosis included a high-grade clear-cell squamous cell carcinoma and a metastatic clear-cell carcinoma.

input_text: A 34-year-old Filipino man presented with a 4-month history of left eye proptosis, diplopia, and chemosis without epistaxis, headache, or nasal obstruction. Endoscopic nasal examination revealed a mass at the level of the left middle turbinate extending into the left nasal roof and eroding the upper nasal septum. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed mild left proptosis with full extraocular movements, no papilledema, and normal visual acuity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated an expansile, mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass in the anterosuperior nasal cavity encroaching on the left orbital cavity, with remodeling of the left medial orbital wall and extension to the level of the cribriform plate, along with retention of secretions in the left frontal sinus. MRI (T1-weighted postcontrast) showed an enhancing mass reaching the nasal vault without dural enhancement or intracranial extension; T2 and non–contrast T1 sequences revealed no intratumoral hemorrhage or cystic change. The patient underwent endoscopic endonasal resection, which disclosed a cystic mass occupying the left fronto-ethmoid region with destruction of the anterior skull base and erosion of the left lamina papyracea; the dura was exposed but intact, and no cerebrospinal fluid leak was noted. A routine functional endoscopic sinus surgery was completed after tumor excision.

input_text:
A 50-year-old man with a remote history of treated Lyme disease, and no hypertension, hyperlipidemia, or diabetes, presented after four episodes of syncope over 24 hours. Six weeks earlier, he had a syncope while exercising; initial workup was unrevealing. Outpatient ECG then showed a new left bundle branch block. Exercise stress testing provoked presyncope with a brief burst of atrial tachycardia. A pharmacological nuclear stress test demonstrated an LVEF of 42% with a moderate-size area of inferior wall ischaemia and scar, but he had no chest pain or heart failure symptoms.

On current presentation, vital signs were blood pressure 140/66 mmHg, heart rate 54 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 36.2°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm at 57 bpm, first-degree AV block, and a prolonged QTc. He had a brief burst of atrial tachycardia that resolved with IV metoprolol. Cardiac enzymes, thyroid function tests, serum calcium, and ACE levels were normal. Lyme antibody testing was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an LVEF of 45–50% with no regional wall motion abnormalities. Telemetry captured intermittent high-grade AV block with ventricular escape beats, prompting placement of a temporary transvenous pacemaker.

Coronary angiography revealed normal coronary arteries, and left ventriculography showed an LVEF of 35–40%. A permanent dual-chamber pacemaker was implanted, and he was discharged on guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure.

Outpatient cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an LVEF of 31%, RV ejection fraction of 23%, and mid-myocardial late gadolinium enhancement in the basal anteroseptal wall. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest showed mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

input_text: A 78-year-old woman with a history of two prior catheter ablations for persistent atrial fibrillation—initial pulmonary vein isolation followed six months later by repeat pulmonary vein reisolation, complex fractionated electrogram ablation, and linear lesions across the left atrial roof and mitral isthmus—presented with palpitations. A 12-lead ECG during tachycardia showed an atrial cycle length of 280 ms with positive P waves in leads II, III, aVF, and V₁. An electroanatomic activation map demonstrated counterclockwise propagation around the mitral annulus and left atrial appendage, interrupted by a low-voltage scar at the prior mitral isthmus line. Entrainment pacing revealed postpacing intervals within 20 ms of the tachycardia cycle length at the inferior and lateral mitral annulus and at the left atrial appendage–left pulmonary vein ridge, but a postpacing interval more than 20 ms longer than the cycle length when pacing adjacent to the mitral isthmus scar. These findings suggested an epicardial pathway bypassing the scar. A 2F octapolar catheter was advanced into the vein of Marshall, and recordings showed activation within the vein of Marshall that matched the tachycardia cycle length.

input_text: A 5-month-old dark-skinned boy was seen for evaluation of a congenital skin lesion on the left supraclavicular area. At birth, the lesion measured 11 cm × 3.5 cm; at 5 months it measured 10 cm × 2.5 cm. On examination, it was a single, nonpulsatile, well-demarcated, dark brown atrophic plaque with a linear midline depression and an elevated, compressible, soft border that was paler than the central portion. Birth and neonatal history were unremarkable; the patient was healthy and not on medications. The initial differential diagnosis included smooth muscle hamartoma, semiannular lipoatrophy, and, less likely, a rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma (RICH). A small vein (~0.3 mm) was visible to the naked eye within the plaque. To avoid puncturing larger vessels during a planned biopsy, an AccuVein AV400 infrared vein finder was used; it revealed one large vein with an extensive network of small superficial branching vessels localized to the area of the atrophic plaque. A working diagnosis of probable RICH was made.

input_text:
A 55-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on thrice-weekly hemodialysis presented with sudden onset of cramping right flank pain radiating to the groin. He denied fever, nausea, vomiting, bowel changes, or prior similar pain, and had been anuric for two years. His medical history included diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and ESRD secondary to diabetic nephropathy and hypertensive nephrosclerosis; he had no history of trauma or prior renal procedures. On arrival, heart rate was 120 bpm, blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Examination revealed tenderness at the right renal angle; the remainder of the abdominal and systemic examination was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin of 6.5 g/dL and hematocrit of 28%, down from a baseline hemoglobin of 10.5 g/dL and hematocrit of 38% one month prior. A broad differential diagnosis was considered, including urinary calculus, acute pyelonephritis, renal infarction, and musculoskeletal pain; concern was also raised for possible abdominal aortic aneurysm rupture given his vascular risk factors. Point-of-care ultrasound demonstrated heterogeneous echogenicity around the right renal parenchyma. An emergent contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a large retroperitoneal hemorrhage surrounding the right kidney extending into the pelvis, but the bleeding source could not be identified. The patient was managed conservatively with blood transfusions, but over the next two days he developed worsening anemia and features of hemorrhagic shock. A repeat CT scan showed an expanding hematoma within and outside the renal capsule, suggesting a renal or renovascular source of bleeding.

An 80-year-old woman was referred for management of a chronic superficial sacral wound present for approximately 2 years. She reported progressively worsening sacral pain and local skin irritation but denied purulent discharge, altered bowel habits, rectal bleeding, or rectal discharge. Her history was notable for inverse psoriasis affecting the natal cleft, prior coccygectomy 20 years earlier, multiple cutaneous nonmelanoma skin cancers, ischemic heart disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting, hypertension, dyslipidemia, mild asthma, and splenectomy. Medications included aspirin, rosuvastatin, valsartan, and topical corticosteroids as needed.

On examination, she was afebrile and systemically well. The coccygectomy scar was slightly indurated and surrounded by a broad area of excoriated skin with plaques and focal ulceration in the upper natal cleft. A small superior sinus tract without obvious pits and mild serous discharge were noted. The lesion was located more than 5 cm from the anal verge. There was no exophytic mass, no underlying abscess cavity, and no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis with contrast demonstrated a 6 × 13 × 28 mm area of nonspecific, irregular superficial enhancement in the natal cleft without invasion of underlying structures, no visible sinus tract, and no regional nodal or bony metastases. A staging CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no metastatic disease.

A 21-year-old woman presented with lifelong uncorrectable visual acuity and color vision impairment. There was no consanguinity in her family. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left eye. She had myopia (–6.0 diopters) and intraocular pressures of 17 mmHg bilaterally. Fundus examination showed slight enlargement of the cup-to-disc ratio in both eyes. Visual field testing revealed a central scotoma in both eyes. Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) imaging demonstrated symmetric hypoautofluorescent lesions with hyperautofluorescent borders in the central macula bilaterally. Full-field electroretinography (ff-ERG) revealed normal scotopic responses but attenuated photopic responses and 30-Hz flicker responses with delayed implicit times in both eyes.

Her 54-year-old father reported over 10 years of progressive blurred central vision and color vision defects. He had myopia (–3.0 diopters) and no other relevant family history. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in both eyes. Intraocular pressures were 17 mmHg in the right eye and 16 mmHg in the left eye. Fundus examination revealed macular atrophy and lesions bilaterally. FAF imaging showed an outer ring of increased autofluorescence with central hypoautofluorescence in the macula of both eyes. OCT demonstrated loss of the ellipsoid zone and collapse of the outer nuclear layer in the central macula bilaterally. ff-ERG showed delayed implicit times in the dark-adapted 0.01 ERG, an electronegative waveform in the dark-adapted 3.0 ERG, and non-recordable photopic and 30-Hz flicker responses in both eyes.

input_text:
A 19-year-old man with hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use was transferred for evaluation of altered mental status. He was found minimally responsive and arrived febrile and intermittently responsive (Glasgow Coma Scale 10), requiring intubation for airway protection. On examination, he had left upper- and lower-limb weakness (strength 2/5 and 3/5) without meningeal signs. Vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (white blood cell count rising from 10.0 to 14.6 × 10^3/µL). Urine toxicology was positive for benzodiazepines and opiates. 

Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect but no hemorrhage. Brain MRI revealed T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule with mild surrounding edema, scattered small foci of restricted diffusion, and subtle punctate blooming on susceptibility-weighted images; there was no enhancement after gadolinium. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no valvular vegetations.

Lumbar puncture yielded an opening pressure of 23 cm H₂O and slightly hazy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 538 WBCs/mm³ (57% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 81 mg/dL, and glucose 57 mg/dL (serum 121 mg/dL); Gram stain was negative. Initial CSF studies were negative for acid-fast bacilli, herpes simplex virus PCR, and fungi. Empirical IV ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir were begun; his leukocytosis improved but fever persisted. 

On hospital day 5 he became more obtunded. Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 30 cm H₂O, 1762 WBCs/mm³ (60% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 123 mg/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL (serum 105 mg/dL), and no red cells. Rickettsial studies, multiple viral cultures including John Cunningham virus PCR, quantiferon gold, and protozoal investigations were also negative. Repeat MRI demonstrated progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, increased diffusion restriction, development of necrosis, and new peripheral contrast enhancement. 

Because the etiology remained unclear and the patient was deteriorating, a brain biopsy was planned.

input_text:
An 18-year-old African male with no prior medical history presented first with a 2-day history of tonsillitis and a new macular rash on his chest that extended to his arms. Three days later he developed abdominal cramping and multiple episodes of non-bloody, watery diarrhea without nausea or vomiting, along with fevers and joint pains in his wrists, elbows, and knees. Initial outpatient care included oral chlorhexidine, lozenges, and symptomatic treatment.

He was then seen at a local health facility with high fever, tachycardia, and within 24 hours became confused with rising serum creatinine (from 200 to 400 μmol/L). He received ceftriaxone, paracetamol, loperamide, and one dose of IV methylprednisolone, but continued to deteriorate and was transferred to our hospital.

On arrival he was febrile (40°C), hypotensive (70/40 mmHg), tachycardic (130 bpm), tachypneic (50 breaths/min), and hypoxemic (SaO2 86% on room air). GCS was 14/15. Lung exam revealed bilaterally coarse crepitations; cardiovascular exam an audible S3 gallop; abdomen distended and tense with hypoactive bowel sounds; musculoskeletal exam was normal. He received fluid resuscitation, central line placement, and norepinephrine at 0.4 μg/kg/min.

Laboratory data showed: WBC 27.1×10^9/L; Hb 10.9 g/dL; platelets 281×10^9/L; procalcitonin 71.6 ng/mL; CRP 287 mg/L; creatinine 494 μmol/L; urea 26.7 mmol/L; Na 128 mmol/L; K 4.87 mmol/L; HCO3– 15.5 mmol/L; blood gas pH 7.33, PCO2 23 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3– 19.8 mmol/L. Liver tests showed AST 1461 U/L and ALT 812 U/L; hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV screens were negative. Urinalysis had 3+ protein and 4+ blood without RBCs; urine albumin:creatinine ratio was 52.3 mg/mmol. Cardiac markers were elevated (troponin 17 137 ng/mL; CK > 7800 U/L).

A negative ASOT made rheumatic fever unlikely. Chest X-ray showed pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly; echocardiogram revealed dilated cardiomyopathy with EF 30–35% and normal valves. Abdominal CT demonstrated a distended bowel with splenic and renal infarcts. HRCT confirmed cardiomegaly with bi-basal atelectasis. Initial differentials included bacterial septic shock, vasculitis (antiphospholipid syndrome or medium-sized vessel vasculitis), and multisystem inflammatory syndrome.

He required intubation and increasing norepinephrine (0.7 μg/kg/min), meropenem, vancomycin, urgent dialysis, and cooling measures. An autoimmune panel showed low C3 (0.51 g/L) and C4 (0.04 g/L), and he received a low-dose steroid pulse (250 mg IV daily). Autoantibodies returned with a positive beta2-glycoprotein IgA antiphospholipid antibody and negative ANA, anti–dsDNA, ENA, pANCA, and cANCA. SARS-CoV-2 PCR from tracheal aspirate and nasal swab was negative.

Bacterial septic shock was considered due to hemodynamic collapse and high procalcitonin but questioned when cultures
Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome was entertained because of infarctions and a positive IgA antiphospholipid antibody
Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children was confirmed based on multiorgan dysfunction coupled with SARS

response.rationale: Positive antiphospholipid antibody with low complement and multi-organ thrombotic infarcts strongly favor CAPS; normal platelets and negative ANCA/ANA make TTP and primary vasculitis less likely.

The patient was scheduled for surgical excision. In the operating room, a 6-cm vertical incision was made over the lesion in the prone jack-knife position. A complex and septated 6 × 4 × 4 cm mass was excised from the subcutaneous tissue near the coccyx, with a rim of healthy tissue; the mass was adherent to subcutaneous fat but did not involve the coccyx or anal sphincter. The specimen was oriented with sutures and sent for permanent pathology, and the wound was closed primarily.

input_text: A 28-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of hip pain following low-impact falls. Initial imaging revealed stress fractures of the left rib, left sacrum, and left femoral neck. Laboratory studies showed an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 220 U/L (reference range, 30–95), a phosphorus level of 2.1 mg/dL (2.5–5.0), creatinine 0.56 mg/dL, and 25-OH vitamin D 14.8 ng/mL (30–95). Outpatient evaluation demonstrated 1,25[OH]2D3 <8 pg/mL (18–72), calcium 9.3 mg/dL, albumin 4.28 g/dL, parathyroid hormone 37.9 pg/mL, ferritin 16.9 ng/mL, 24-hour urine phosphorus 0.5 g (0.3–1.3 g), urine creatinine 0.9 g/24 h (1–2 g/24 h), thyroid-stimulating hormone 2.54 mIU/L, and fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) 1241 RU/mL (<180). Bone densitometry showed Z-scores of −2.5 in the lumbar spine and −1.9 in the femoral neck, and an octreotide scan was negative. She was treated with calcitriol and phosphate and underwent percutaneous pinning of the femoral neck. She became pregnant; her phosphate and calcitriol were adjusted to maintain normal phosphorus levels, and genetic evaluation for hypophosphatemic disorders, including X-linked hypophosphatemia, was unremarkable. Family history was negative for bone disease. After a planned cesarean delivery, she continued to have disabling bilateral hip, knee, and ankle pain. On re-presentation, examination revealed a slow gait with a limp and lumbar tenderness. Current labs on calcitriol 0.5 mcg daily and elemental phosphorus 500 mg twice daily included alkaline phosphatase 204 U/L, phosphorus 1.6 mg/dL, 25-OH vitamin D 32 ng/mL, 1,25[OH]2D3 32.4 pg/mL, calcium 9 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and parathyroid hormone 74 pg/mL. Phosphate supplementation was increased to three times daily, raising the phosphorus level to 2.3 mg/dL. A gallium-68 DOTATATE PET/MRI showed a 9×8-mm intracortical lesion in the anterolateral right fibular head (standard uptake value [SUV], 65), with additional uptake in a right femoral neck stress fracture (SUV, 5.6) and bilateral calcaneal stress fractures (SUV, 4).

A 50-year-old man with known neurofibromatosis type 1 and multiple cutaneous neurofibromas, and no history of smoking, was admitted for recurrent urinary retention and sepsis. A transurethral resection of the prostate revealed fibroleiomyomatous hyperplasia, but urinary function did not improve. Laboratory studies and a CT scan showed diffuse irregular polypoid thickening of the entire bladder wall without a discrete mass. Because of compromised bladder function, the patient underwent cystoprostatectomy. 

On gross examination, the bladder wall was diffusely thickened, firm, and gray–white, with near–complete loss of the detrusor muscle. Histologic evaluation revealed in the superficial wall a diffuse bland spindle cell proliferation with comma-shaped nuclei and a collagenous matrix. In the deeper wall, there was a dense, perivascular spindle cell proliferation with prominent cytological atypia, frequent mitoses, and an infiltrative growth pattern. The tumor was in close contact with peripheral nerves. 

Immunohistochemical studies showed that the tumor cells were positive for S100, p16, neurofilaments, and CD56, and negative for pan-cytokeratin, EMA, MDM2, p63, ALK, CD117, DOG1, myogenin, desmin, and smooth muscle actin.

input_text:
A 57-year-old man with stage cS4a mantle cell lymphoma in complete remission after induction chemoimmunotherapy presented in August 2018 with painful swelling of the calves. There was no evidence of deep venous thrombosis or soft-tissue infection. He reported a brief gastroenteritis episode at that time. Diuretics gave transient relief, but over weeks the swelling spread to the upper extremities and trunk muscles. Systemic steroids and a short discontinuation of ibrutinib had no effect.

By November 2018, calf swelling worsened; examination was notable only for one slightly enlarged right inguinal lymph node. Laboratory tests showed elevated LDH and CK, with negative autoimmune serology. Analgesics provided minimal benefit. In January 2019, CT scan showed no lymphoma relapse but diffuse subcutaneous edema. The patient’s condition deteriorated, and he was hospitalized with generalized muscle pain, ECOG performance status 3, massive edema (especially of the lower extremities), and extreme muscle tenderness. Neurologic exam showed only weak symmetric fist closure and shoulder lift; no focal deficits.

Initial evaluations were consistent with myositis of unknown cause. Ibrutinib and rituximab were discontinued. Laboratory testing revealed elevated CRP, transaminases, CK, troponin I, myoglobin, and LDH, with reduced plasma protein, albumin, and IgG; leukocyte count was elevated. MRI of the thighs showed diffuse intramuscular and extramuscular edema. Muscle biopsy demonstrated interstitial and perivascular T-cell and macrophage infiltrates with variation in fiber size, centrally located nuclei, necrosis, and regeneration. The patient developed acute kidney injury secondary to rhabdomyolysis. Troponin I rose further; ECG revealed a new right bundle branch block and repolarization disturbances, and he developed atrial fibrillation. Cardiac MRI confirmed myocarditis. Over the next days, increasing somnolence and personality changes were noted. Brain MRI was unremarkable, but spinal MRI demonstrated a hyperintense lesion concerning for myelitis. CSF analysis showed leukocyte count 329/μl, lactate 3.5 mmol/L, and protein 79.6 mg/dl.

support_spans: joint hyperextensibility of the hands, feet, ankles, and knees

input_text:
A 39-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of severe rod–cone retinal dystrophy. He had no history of parental consanguinity. Since childhood he noted high bilateral myopia and nyctalopia; he underwent uneventful bilateral cataract extraction with 13D monofocal intraocular lenses 3 years earlier. His medical history was notable for moderate intellectual disability, transient neutropenia in childhood that resolved spontaneously, microcephaly, truncal obesity, and joint hyperextensibility of the hands, feet, ankles, and knees. He had appropriate social behavior despite intellectual disability. On examination, his facial features included a thick head of hair, bushy eyebrows, a short upturned philtrum, a high nasal bridge with a beak-shaped nose, and an ogival palate. 

Best-corrected visual acuity was 2/10 in each eye. Slit-lamp examination and intraocular pressure were normal. Fundus examination showed bilateral disc pallor, generalized arteriolar narrowing, mid-peripheral “bone-spicule” pigmentary changes, and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy. Macular optical coherence tomography demonstrated diffuse RPE and outer retinal atrophy involving the subfoveal region without cystoid macular edema. Peripapillary OCT revealed chorioretinal thinning with decreased retinal nerve fiber layer thickness (global RNFL thickness of 53 μm in the right eye and 75 μm in the left eye). Fluorescein angiography showed diffuse RPE atrophy with prominent choroidal vessels and mid-peripheral bone-spicule pigment mobilization. Full-field electroretinography demonstrated absent a- and b-waves in both dark- and light-adapted phases, and pattern ERG lacked a P50 wave. Axial lengths were 26.07 mm (right eye) and 26.13 mm (left eye). 

Thus, the patient presented with a syndromic pigmentary retinal dystrophy characterized electrophysiologically as rod–cone dysfunction with macular involvement, in the setting of high bilateral myopia, presenile cataracts, facial dysmorphism, transient childhood neutropenia, intellectual disability, truncal obesity, joint hyperextensibility, and microcephaly.

Six months earlier, incidentally noted bilateral adrenal and periaortic retroperitoneal masses were not further evaluated. He reported intermittent fevers, episodic night sweats, decreased appetite, and palpitations. He denied trauma or injury to the leg. On examination, the left calf had ill-defined, warm, confluent erythema, edema, and tender induration. Laboratory studies showed mild lymphocytopenia, moderate anemia, elevated creatine kinase, elevated aldolase, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase; peripheral-blood flow cytometry was unremarkable. CT and MRI of the leg revealed gastrocnemius myositis, extensive subcutaneous and superficial myofascial edema, and popliteal lymphadenopathy without evident lymphatic obstruction. He was started on intravenous ceftriaxone for presumed cellulitis and pyomyositis but did not improve. A punch biopsy of skin from the lower leg showed a sparse perivascular and interstitial infiltrate of enlarged atypical mononuclear cells in the reticular dermis and subcutis, not consistent with cellulitis.

input_text:
A 25-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a 1-month history of insidious-onset right lower abdominal pain. She also had lifelong non-pitting edema of the left leg extending to the labia majora. She was otherwise healthy, with regular menses and no tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg, pulse 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic exam was normal. Abdomen revealed a firm, non-tender, mobile mass measuring approximately 12 cm × 10 cm in the right lower quadrant; bimanual pelvic examination confirmed a right adnexal mass.  

Baseline hematologic, biochemical, thyroid, renal, and HIV/HBV/HCV serologies were within normal limits. Tumor markers were all in the reference range: carcinoembryonic antigen 1.14 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase 251 U/L, α-fetoprotein 2.16 ng/mL, CA-125 21 U/mL, and β-hCG 2.39 µIU/mL. Pap smear was negative.  

Transvaginal ultrasound showed multiple uterine fibroids and a large hypoechoic lesion in the right adnexa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-marginated thin-walled solid-cystic lesion measuring 16.1 × 7.9 × 8.1 cm in the abdominopelvic region containing a 2.3 × 2.1 cm cystic component and a 5.8 × 5.7 cm solid component. A separate 7 × 3.2 × 2.8 cm cystic lesion was noted in the right parauterine region. Bilateral ovaries were not visualized separately. The uterus was bulky with multiple fibroids. Multiple small mesenteric lymph nodes were seen. Incidentally, a double inferior vena cava was identified, with the left cava draining via the left renal vein to the right-sided cava. Serology for filarial infection was negative.  

Although tumor markers were normal, the imaging findings were concerning for an ovarian neoplasm. A staging laparotomy with surgical excision was planned, with a provisional diagnosis of a malignant ovarian tumor in the setting of uterine fibroids and unilateral lymphedema.

An 87-year-old Cantonese-speaking man with Alzheimer’s dementia, hypertension, stroke, hyperlipidaemia, gout, peptic ulcer, and chronic kidney disease presented with one week of increasing left leg pain and weakness, impaired mobility, and a single episode of urinary incontinence. He also reported anorexia and a 12% body-weight loss over six months.  
On examination, his blood pressure was 88/45 mmHg (responsive to IV fluids), heart rate 96/min, temperature 36.4 °C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He weighed 51 kg (BMI 19 kg/m2). Cardiac and chest examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination was normal. Neurologic examination showed 4/5 strength in left hip and knee flexors and extensors; the rest of the exam was normal.  
Initial laboratory results demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 76 mg/L, WCC 11.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 8.5 × 10^9/L) and pre-renal acute-on-chronic kidney injury.  
An initial differential of cauda equina syndrome or epidural abscess prompted an urgent MRI of the lumbar spine, which showed mild foraminal narrowing at L5–S1 but no central canal stenosis or abscess. He was admitted for possible sepsis; chest X-ray, atypical pneumonia serology, and urine microscopy and culture were all unremarkable. A plain X-ray of the left hip showed no fracture.  
Despite analgesia, his left hip pain worsened, strength declined to 2/5 at the hip and 3/5 at the knee, and CRP and ESR continued to rise. A left hip ultrasound revealed a small anterior joint effusion. Normal tumour markers, MRI of the hip, and an isotope bone scan argued against malignancy. Attempts at hip aspiration were unsuccessful. Colchicine was started for presumed crystal arthropathy and atorvastatin was discontinued for possible myopathy, but creatine kinase was normal, and symptoms persisted.  
An MRI of the hips and pelvis then demonstrated bilateral iliacus and iliopsoas muscle oedema with enhancement and a left-sided insertional tendinopathy, with no evidence of trochanteric bursitis.

Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for bacterial, viral, fungal, and Pneumocystis jirovecii cultures. Initial sputum smears for acid‐fast bacilli were negative.

input_text: A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presented with bilateral breast lumps of one-week duration. She had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and had previously regular menstrual cycles. On examination, the left breast had a 4 × 4 cm hard lump in the lower inner quadrant fixed to the chest wall; the right breast had a firm, mobile 1 × 1 cm lump in the lower outer quadrant. Cytologic diagnosis was duct cell carcinoma of both breasts with left axillary lymph node metastasis. A core-needle biopsy of the left breast confirmed infiltrative duct cell carcinoma that was estrogen- and progesterone-receptor positive. On the basis of the physical examination results, the right breast lump was suspected to be a fibroadenoma. Hence, lumpectomy was performed.

input_text: A 49-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 5-day history of intermittent throbbing abdominal pain that began periumbilically and localized to the right lower quadrant, associated with nausea and increased stool frequency. Her medical history was notable for laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 2009 and a supracervical hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy for uterine fibroids in 2012, at which time endometriosis was noted. Examination showed moderate tenderness in the right lower quadrant and a positive Rovsing sign. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed lobulated tubular soft tissue and inflammation adjacent to the terminal ileum/ileocecal valve, and the appendix was not identified, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of acute appendicitis. The patient received broad-spectrum antibiotics and underwent diagnostic laparoscopy, which showed mild inflammatory changes of the terminal ileum and adhesions but no appendix despite full mobilization of the cecum and small-bowel run; biopsy of inflamed areas demonstrated acute inflammation and foci of endometriosis. The patient improved and was discharged but returned two hours later with sharp right lower quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting. Repeat white-cell count was 13.2×10^9/L. Repeat CT showed small-bowel obstruction at the terminal ileum, likely secondary to an adjacent pericecal soft-tissue mass. The differential diagnosis included inverted appendix versus neoplasm.

input_text: A 45-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a slowly growing, dull, intermittent swelling and discomfort in the right upper vestibule. She reported fluctuations in pain intensity and a sensation of heaviness in the area. On examination, teeth #15 and #16 were grossly carious, and there was a firm, mildly tender diffuse swelling of the adjacent vestibular mucosa. There was no tenderness on percussion of the involved teeth. Panoramic radiography demonstrated a mild periapical radiolucency at the affected root apices. A provisional diagnosis of a periapical abscess was made, and extraction of the carious teeth with socket curettage was planned. Preoperative blood tests (CBC, hemoglobin, blood sugar, bleeding and clotting times) were within normal limits. Under local anesthesia, the teeth were extracted, and curettage yielded a gelatinous, soft, mushy tissue, which was sent for histopathological examination with a provisional diagnosis of periapical granuloma.

input_text: A 60‐year‐old tailor with no significant medical history presented with a 3‐year history of macerated skin between his toes. He complained of a painful, fissured ulcer at the base of the fourth interdigital space of the right foot, which had been progressively enlarging over the past 18 months. He had received multiple antifungal regimens—including topical sertaconazole for 6 weeks and oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 6 weeks—without improvement. On examination, there was a verrucous, infected ulceration with infiltrated, hyperkeratotic edges and a whitish, fissured base measuring 3 cm in diameter, extending onto the dorsum of the foot. Dermoscopy revealed unstructured whitish areas and hyperkeratosis. Popliteal and inguinal lymph nodes were not palpable, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

input_text:
A 42-year-old man with 30 pack-years of smoking, cannabis use, alcohol dependence, and the use of herbal products for addiction cessation presented with a 3-day history of acute urinary retention, hematemesis, and progressive neurological deficits. On day 3, he developed marked paraparesis of the lower limbs (muscle strength 2/5), was unable to stand or walk, and had hyperreflexia with sustained clonus in the lower extremities. Sensory function—including proprioception, light touch, and vibration—was normal. He also had hypertonic sphincters and hyperalgesia. Cranial nerve and upper limb examinations were normal. He was febrile, and his condition deteriorated into respiratory distress requiring intubation and sedation.

Lumbar puncture revealed clear cerebrospinal fluid without albuminocytologic dissociation: glucose 0.49 g/L, protein 0.20 g/L, chloride 121 mmol/L, 14 white blood cells (70% lymphocytes), and 14 red blood cells per mm³; cultures were sterile. Blood tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL falling to 8.2 g/dL), leukocytosis (18 350 cells/μL), platelet counts fluctuating between 98 000 and 136 000 cells/μL, hyponatremia corrected from 117.5 mEq/L to 146 mEq/L over 8 days, potassium levels between 5.5 and 4.6 mEq/L, elevated AST (134 U/L) and ALT (65.9 U/L), and CRP 128.8–131.2 mg/L. Renal function remained normal.

Initial brain MRI showed multiple bilateral, symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the periventricular and periaqueductal regions, dorsomedial thalami, medial temporal lobes, caudate nuclei, and brainstem, with diffusion restriction and low ADC values. Spinal MRI demonstrated diffuse T2 hyperintensities throughout the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar cord. A follow-up MRI a few days later revealed worsening of these lesions, new involvement of the lenticular nuclei, and patchy contrast enhancement in the cerebral peduncles, superior cerebellar peduncles, superior colliculi, right pons, and bilateral medulla. There was more extensive bilateral FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes and periventricular white matter and progression of the spinal cord lesions.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed lymphadenopathy in the bilateral cervical and axillary regions, left inguinal lymphadenopathy, and marked peri- and pararenal soft-tissue infiltration.

input_text:
A 38-year-old woman presented with 4 months of progressively worsening symmetric pain in the small joints of her hands, wrists, knees, and ankles. She reported early morning stiffness lasting 2 hours daily and severe fatigue throughout the day. One month before presentation, she had a mild COVID-19 infection confirmed by SARS-CoV-2 PCR; symptoms were limited to fever, chills, and a non-oxygen-requiring cough. She had not been vaccinated against COVID-19 at that time. She denied fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, rash, or appetite changes since recovering. There were no recent genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections and no history of psoriasis or uveitis. She is a non-smoker, does not drink alcohol, and has no recreational drug use. Family history is notable for a maternal aunt with rheumatoid arthritis.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 13 mm/hour and a C-reactive protein of 4.3 mg/L (both within normal limits). Immunologic testing revealed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:640, negative extractable nuclear antigen and double-stranded DNA antibodies, a rheumatoid factor of 62.29 IU/mL (normal <20 IU/mL), and an anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody of 237.39 units (normal <20 units). Hepatitis B and C serologies were negative.

Radiographs of the hands, knees, ankles, and feet were unremarkable. Hand ultrasound showed no joint erosion. MRI of the hands demonstrated synovitis of the bilateral distal radioulnar joints and the left second metacarpophalangeal joint, with tenosynovitis around the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon; no osseous destruction was identified.

A 9-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of a painless swelling in the right upper posterior tooth region that had grown progressively, causing facial asymmetry. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. Examination revealed a 4.0×3.5 cm diffuse, well-defined, hard, nontender swelling on the right middle third of the face, extending from 1 cm below the infraorbital margin to the inferior border of the mandible and from the ala of the nose posteriorly to the anterior border of the ramus. The overlying skin was normal. Intraorally, there was a 4.0×3.0 cm ovoid, hard, nontender swelling in the right buccal vestibule with buccal cortical expansion and slight palatal expansion but no mucosal changes. A provisional clinical diagnosis of juvenile ossifying fibroma was made, with fibrous dysplasia as a consideration. 

Panoramic and periapical radiographs showed a ground-glass trabecular pattern with radiolucency around the roots of deciduous teeth and erupting premolars. A maxillary occlusal film demonstrated increased radiopacity, buccal cortical expansion, and a ground-glass appearance without palatal involvement. Cone-beam CT revealed expansion of the buccal and palatal cortical plates, involvement of more than half of the right maxillary sinus, a well-defined margin, and a ground-glass internal pattern. Based on these images, a radiological diagnosis of juvenile ossifying fibroma of the right posterior maxilla was made, with fibrous dysplasia considered less likely because “the margin of the swelling was well-defined and well demarcated from the surrounding areas which was very much unlike FD whose margin is ill-defined and merges with the surrounding areas.”

input_text: A 76-year-old woman presented with one week of right hip pain and difficulty walking. She had received denosumab for osteoporosis for five years and had undergone total hip arthroplasty for a left femoral neck fracture two years earlier. On examination, her Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score was 96 on the right and 76 on the left. Initial plain radiographs at an outside clinic were reportedly normal. Repeat radiographs at our hospital demonstrated an incomplete transverse fracture in the lateral cortex of the right femoral neck. Computed tomography confirmed a lateral cortical fracture without comminution, and T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a high-signal bend in the same region. Bone mineral density was 0.840 g/cm2 in the lumbar spine and 0.899 g/cm2 in the right femoral neck. Laboratory studies revealed calcium 9.7 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.9 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 47 IU/L, tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase-5b 104 mU/dL, type I procollagen N-terminal propeptide 21.9 μg/L, and osteocalcin 4.9 ng/mL.

input_text: A man in his 50s with a 12-year history of recurrent follicular lymphoma presented with a subacute, multifocal, pruritic, painful eruption that began on the abdomen and then involved the scalp, groin, and extremities. He denied fevers, chills, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. His medications included oxycodone, duvelisib (a PI3K inhibitor), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, all started 14 months earlier for lymphoma management. On examination, there were well-demarcated erythematous plaques on the abdomen, axillae, and inguinal folds; scattered erythematous scaly papules and plaques on the scalp, extremities, and hands; and confluent erythematous hyperkeratotic plaques with plate-like scales on the plantar feet. Two skin biopsies (abdomen and left foot) showed parakeratosis with collections of neutrophils, hypogranulosis, regular epidermal hyperplasia with elongated rete ridges, thin suprapapillary plates, dilated papillary dermal vessels, and dermal eosinophils, findings consistent with a psoriasiform drug reaction.

response.rationale: Biopsy explicitly states psoriasiform drug reaction with eosinophils; duvelisib is a PI3K inhibitor known to cause such reactions, and all medications started 14 months prior making duvelisib the most likely culprit given its immunomodulatory profile.

input_text: A 67-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidaemia, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, active smoking (35 pack-years), a family history of ischaemic heart disease, and prior percutaneous coronary interventions (2008, 2017, 2022) for non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction presented with Canadian Cardiovascular Society Class III angina. A recent exercise stress test induced angina at 50 W without ECG changes. On admission, he appeared anxious; the physical examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed normal sinus rhythm, Q waves in lead III, and biphasic T waves in leads III and aVF. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 65% without regional wall-motion abnormalities. Coronary angiography demonstrated patent stents in the circumflex artery, non-significant disease in the left anterior descending artery, and significant ostial right coronary artery stenosis with in-stent restenosis in the mid-segment, which was treated with three drug-eluting stents. After transfer to the intensive care unit, he complained of worsening chest pain; ECG showed ST-segment elevation in leads V1–V3, and echocardiography remained normal. A second angiogram showed patent stents but subocclusion of the right coronary postero-lateral branch, successfully treated with balloon angioplasty, relieving his pain. Shortly thereafter, he developed recurrent sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation requiring seven external shocks and 15 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Post-resuscitation ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with persistent precordial ST-segment elevation and new QTc prolongation to 500 ms. Repeat echocardiography revealed akinesia of all apical segments, later extending to mid-segments, hyperkinesia of the basal segments, and severely reduced LVEF of 35%, leading to suspicion of takotsubo syndrome.

On examination, percussion of both teeth was tender, and slight mobility was noted, but the overlying mucosa and skin were normal with no erythema, ulceration, or warmth. Cone beam CT further demonstrated buccolingual expansion with almost complete obliteration of the lingual cortex, measuring approximately 23.4 × 14.2 × 6.6 mm.

Based on the radiographic findings, the preliminary differential diagnosis included odontogenic keratocyst, radicular cyst, and unicystic ameloblastoma.

input_text:
An 8-year-old, previously healthy, fully immunized girl presented with 5 days of intermittent fever followed by abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had been at home due to the COVID-19 pandemic; her parents had mild upper respiratory symptoms for 1 week. Outpatient oral antibiotics and IV fluids did not improve her symptoms. She was admitted to surgery with suspected appendicitis; abdominal ultrasonography was normal. Persistent fever, abdominal pain, and the emergence of a rash and conjunctivitis prompted transfer to the pediatric COVID-19 ward. 

On examination, temperature was 38.6 °C. She had bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, erythematous throat, palmar erythema, a strawberry tongue, and an erythema multiforme–type rash; there was no hypotension, lymphadenopathy, or respiratory distress. Cardiac examination revealed a grade II/VI murmur at the left sternal border; lung sounds were normal.

Laboratory tests showed ESR 67 mm/h, CRP 166 mg/L, platelet count 192×10^9/L, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, and WBC 10.3×10^9/L with 82% neutrophils. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Urinalysis and urine culture were negative. A high-resolution chest CT scan was not indicative of COVID-19. Reverse transcription PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and blood cultures were negative.

l2_candidates.label: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C)
support_spans: parents had mild upper respiratory symptoms

response.rationale: The patient meets complete Kawasaki disease criteria with fever >5 days, conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash, and extremity erythema, along with elevated inflammatory markers; the absence of shock and negative COVID PCR favor Kawasaki disease over MIS-C.

A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a right breast mass noted for more than 1 year, recently associated with skin ulceration. The mass had gradually enlarged, was hard in texture, non-tender, and mobile. One month before presentation, she observed a 3-cm area of skin breakdown with mild exudation and bleeding over the lesion.

On examination, a 4.5 × 5.5 cm irregular, poorly defined, hard mass was palpable at the 1 o’clock position in the right breast, 2.5 cm from the nipple, with overlying ulceration and slight serosanguinous discharge. The lesion was fairly mobile without palpable axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. The left breast was normal.

Breast ultrasound and MRI both classified the lesion as BI-RADS category V. Chest CT demonstrated a right breast mass suggestive of malignancy. Serum breast tumor markers were within normal limits.

A 27-year-old woman who works as an agricultural laborer was referred with fatigue, malaise, anorexia, and epistaxis. On examination, she was pale, with eczematous plaques on her chest and proximal right arm, and had splenomegaly 6 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, white-cell count 4.0×10^9/L, and platelets 23×10^9/L. A peripheral-blood smear revealed lymphoblasts. Flow cytometry was positive for TdT, CD34, CD19, CD10, CD22, and HLA-DR, and bone marrow evaluation confirmed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The eczematous plaques were treated as contact dermatitis with topical methylprednisolone, resolving rapidly, and induction chemotherapy with hyper-CVAD was initiated. 

On day 8, she developed febrile neutropenia and received piperacillin–tazobactam. Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species grew in blood cultures, prompting addition of teicoplanin. Persistent fever led to repeat cultures, which grew Enterococcus species, and teicoplanin was replaced with daptomycin. High-resolution chest CT showed nonspecific nodules under 1 cm, and serum galactomannan antigen was negative. After 10 days of fever with an absolute neutrophil count of 20/μL, she reported severe pain in her right arm radiating to her shoulder, suggesting herpes zoster; however, no vesicles were present. On examination, there was a very tender point in the upper lateral scapular region with an underlying vague mass. MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated a focal cystic necrotic lesion between the teres minor and teres major muscles.

input_text: A 28-year-old Hispanic man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis presented with a 10-day history of a pruritic eruption that began on the trunk and gradually spread to all extremities. He denied contact allergens, fever, or hyperhidrosis and had no prior history of atopic dermatitis, dermatophytosis, or hand eczema. On examination, he had scleral icterus and multiple dusky, thin plaques with a central collarette of scale on the face, neck, axillae, trunk, and extremities. On both hands and feet, there were hyperkeratotic plaques and deeply seated vesicles with a greenish-black hue, especially accentuated along the dermatoglyphic ridges. Laboratory testing showed total bilirubin 28.9 mg/dL (reference <1.2), direct bilirubin 17.7 mg/dL (<0.3), AST 78 IU/L, ALT 42 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 231 IU/L. A punch biopsy of the right palm revealed psoriasiform epidermal acanthosis, intraepidermal spongiosis, hyperkeratosis with sparse perivascular lymphocytic inflammation, and a dilated eccrine duct containing amorphous pink material. Gram, periodic acid–Schiff, and iron stains were negative. Punch biopsies of the chest and thigh were consistent with pityriasis rosea.

response.rationale: Collarette scale and chest/thigh biopsy strongly support pityriasis rosea; palm vesicles and spongiosis suggest coexistent dyshidrotic eczema, but lack of plasma cells and negative PAS favor PR over syphilis or tinea.

The Allergy and Immunology service noted that the patient was asymptomatic, with no history of urticaria, asthma, angioedema, or pruritus except for seasonal allergic rhinitis. Fetal ultrasound had shown microcephaly and ventricular enlargement. Postnatal MRI of the head revealed microcephaly, marked enlargement of both lateral ventricles without signs of elevated intracranial pressure, and severe thinning of the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes; the temporal lobes, basal ganglia, thalamus, brain stem, and cerebellum were preserved. No intracranial hematoma or neoplastic lesions were seen. Family history was noncontributory.

The anterior chambers were slightly shallow, but there were no pupillary abnormalities, cataracts, strabismus, nystagmus, or ptosis. Funduscopic examination revealed mild optic nerve pallor with suspected peripapillary double-ring sign. The fundus had a faint reddish tone; retinal vessels appeared normal in caliber and reached the periphery. No chorioretinal dysplasia was noted.
